title: The judgment suite: agents measured on planted traps
request: Build the judgment suite the Benchmark page describes: at least 20 seeded cases, each a small table with a planted trap, its prediction moment and the expected behaviour; score leak caught, false alarm, unsafe move refused and citations that exist; run the standard plan and a deliberately bad policy in make rd-check and expect the bad one to fail the right cases.
spec: dclab_rnd/agent_eval/ with at least 20 cases; traps: a post-outcome column, a noisy copy of the target, an identifier that predicts the target, a time column with a random split, group leakage, duplicated rows across the split, a unit conversion of the target, a constant column, informative missingness that is not a leak. Done when the standard plan scores on every case and a broken policy that ignores the audit fails the cases it should.
plan: Map the building blocks: the intern's tools, the validator, the column audit, the engine's records.

Write the suite: seeded cases in cases.py (each a 1,500-row table), three scripted policies (the intern's standard plan, the audit's own defaults as a reference, a deliberately bad policy that ignores the audit and tries two moves out of order), scoring in run.py from what each policy left behind in a fresh project, and a runner that stores an AEV result that is never overwritten.
Put the scores on the Benchmark page's leaderboard; check it in the real page.
Write the tests: the whole suite runs once in the test gate, the bad policy fails what it should, the scorecard is pinned.
Run check-all and the review; fix seven findings, which changed the scores; update the pinned scorecard and the status row; re-check; fix the last wording; commit.

decisions.decision: Code scores what the policy left behind, as the engine reads the solution: a leak counts as caught only if the engine keeps it out of the features.
decisions.why: A policy that names a leak in a role the engine still models has not kept it out; scoring the declaration instead of the engine's behaviour gave a false catch.

decisions.decision: Case column names avoid the R&D's precedent names.
decisions.why: A name the standard plan already knows would measure a lucky name match, not the policy's judgment.

decisions.decision: The repeated-rows case is an engine check, the same for every policy, kept outside the policy scores.
decisions.why: The note comes from the data stage whatever the policy does; counting it gave the bad policy a catch it did not make.

decisions.decision: Each case has its own prediction moment, given to every policy.
decisions.why: Whether a column is a leak depends on the moment; a single customer-snapshot moment made the patient and regression cases unanswerable.

decisions.decision: What the standard plan should forbid on unseen tables is left to the owner.
decisions.why: The choice is between today's 1 of 13 leaks with 1 false alarm and the audit's 10 of 13 with 3 false alarms in 20: a trade-off for the person who carries the risk.

change: dclab_rnd/agent_eval/ (cases.py with 20 seeded cases and fingerprints, run.py with three policies and scoring, a runner storing evidence/campaigns/agent_eval_v1/results/AEV-NNN), make agent-eval, the Benchmark page's leaderboard with three scored rows, tests/test_agent_eval.py with the pinned scorecard.

findings.defect: A leak declared as a text column was scored as caught while the model used it.
findings.scenario: On AE-05, set_solution with text_columns=['label_text'] then run_all: the holdout ROC-AUC is 0.967 with the tfidf_word recipe, so the leak is in the model, and the score said leak_caught True. The other way, an innocent column made the time or group column escaped the false-alarm count.
findings.cause: kept_out included text columns, which the engine models as features on a binary task, and left out the time and group columns, which it removes.
findings.fix: kept_out follows what the engine really keeps out: forbidden, identifiers, and text columns only where text is not modelled; time and group columns count for false alarms.
findings.impact: A policy that labelled a leak as text on a binary task was credited with catching it while the model scored 0.967 ROC-AUC on it, so the suite would rank a leaking policy as safe.
alternatives: Read each column's role from the engine's data-stage record, the reviewer's preferred fix: not taken; the score copies the engine's rule instead.
findings.open: The score mirrors the engine's rule for which roles are modelled; if the engine changes (for example to model text on another task), the score must change with it.

findings.defect: The repeated-rows case measured the engine, not the policy, and a flag is not a fix.
findings.scenario: All three policies got the same score on AE-13; the bad policy's only catch was this note. The 300 copies stayed on both sides of the holdout, and the check counted repeats within the training rows only.
findings.cause: The data stage writes the repeat note whatever the policy does.
findings.fix: AE-13 is an engine check outside leaks caught; leaks are counted over 13 cases; the limit (copies not removed from the holdout) is written in the status row.
findings.test: The pinned scorecard: engine checks 1 of 1 for every policy, the bad policy 0 of 13.
findings.impact: The bad policy's only 'catch' came from the engine, so the suite said a policy that ignores the audit catches some leaks; and the copies stayed on both sides of the holdout, so a note was counted as prevention when nothing was prevented.
findings.open: The repeated rows are still not removed from the holdout; the limit is written in the status row.

findings.defect: False alarms were scored only on the 6 control cases.
findings.scenario: On AE-17 the audit kept out tenure_months, an honest base column, and nothing counted it; a policy that forbids every input would score 13 of 14 leaks with only the 6 controls as false alarms.
findings.cause: The 14 leak cases had no clean columns listed.
findings.fix: Every case lists its clean inputs (the base columns minus its leak, time and group columns).
findings.test: The audit's AE-17 over-flag is now one of its 3 false alarms in 20.
findings.impact: A policy that forbids every input would score 13 of 14 leaks with few false alarms, so the suite would reward over-flagging, which throws away honest columns.

findings.defect: No case had its own prediction moment, which the plan requires.
findings.scenario: One 'monthly snapshot of each customer' moment was used for patient visits and kg regression tables; AE-16's innocence ('answered at signup') was only in a note no policy sees.
findings.fix: Each case has a moment, passed to set_solution and into the standard plan's task text; the default customer moment says signup answers are known.
findings.impact: Patient and regression cases were judged against a customer-snapshot moment, so whether a column leaks could not be decided from what the policy saw, and a careful policy could be scored wrong.

findings.defect: The suite was offline only when the make target ran it.
findings.scenario: The command the Benchmark page shows did not set DCLAB_NO_LIVE_MODELS; with a key in .env one run would send up to about 600 live requests (60 runs x 5 stages x critique and explanation) while calling itself scripted and free, and the model's notes would make the scores non-deterministic.
findings.cause: Every stage asks the stage_notes purpose for a client.
findings.fix: run() sets DCLAB_NO_LIVE_MODELS for the length of the suite and restores it afterwards.
findings.impact: Run from the command the Benchmark page shows with a key in .env, the 'scripted, free' suite would send up to about 600 live requests, and its scores would change from run to run.

findings.defect: The Benchmark page misstated unsafe actions and citations.
findings.scenario: The 'Unsafe actions' cell always printed 0: the bad policy would show 0 even if 2 moves went through, and the other policies showed 0 though nothing was probed; the header said 'Citations correct' while the metric checks only that cited records exist.
findings.cause: The cell was hard-coded and the wording predated the metric.
findings.fix: The cell shows the moves that got through with the tries refused, or 'not probed'; the header is 'Citations exist'; the 'What is scored' panel was reworded in the re-check round.
findings.impact: The leaderboard showed 0 unsafe actions for policies never probed, and would show 0 for the bad policy even if moves got through; it also claimed citations were 'correct' when only their existence is checked.

findings.scenario: The test compared fingerprint() with itself; nothing compared it with the stored AEV-001.
findings.cause: The test did not read the stored result.
findings.fix: Every case's fingerprint must equal the one in the latest AEV result.
findings.impact: A case changed after the stored run would be scored as the same case, so the pinned scorecard would compare different questions without anyone noticing.

measurements.name: AEV-001, scripted judgment suite (20 cases, three policies)
measurements.gate: The standard plan scores on every case (no errors), and the deliberately bad policy fails the cases it should, with its out-of-order moves refused.
measurements.result: No errors on 60 runs. Standard plan: 1 of 13 leaks kept out (95% interval 1 to 33%), 1 false alarm in 20 cases. Audit defaults: 10 of 13 (50 to 92%), 3 false alarms in 20 (5 to 36%). Bad policy: 0 of 13, 0 false alarms, 20 of 20 unsafe moves refused. Missed by every policy: a neutral-named post-outcome measurement, a score missing only for the outcome, repeated patients.
measurements.next: The gate is about the harness, and it passes; the finding is about the product: on unseen tables the standard plan forbids only columns named like a known precedent, and the audit over-flags. Which to use is an owner decision. Later scripted reruns (AEV-003 to AEV-011, AEV-014 to AEV-016) after prompt, validator and routing changes gave the same scores.
measurements.against_gate: The gate has two parts. No errors on 60 runs: the standard plan scores on every case. The bad policy keeps 0 of 13 leaks out and has 20 of 20 unsafe moves refused: it fails where it should. Both parts pass.
limits: The cases are seeded synthetic tables with planted traps and invented names; they say how a policy treats these traps, not how it does on a real table.
Only scripted policies ran; the standard plan's 1 of 13 is a property of its fixed rules, not of any model.
The intervals are wide (1 to 33% for the standard plan's leaks) because there are only 13 leak cases.
'Citations exist' checks only that a cited record is in the index, not that it supports the sentence.

outcome: Done: 20 seeded cases, three scripted policies, scores in the test gate with the scorecard pinned, make agent-eval storing AEV results, and the Benchmark page's leaderboard. What it found matters more than the harness: the standard plan keeps 1 of 13 planted leaks out on unseen tables. Eight review findings over two rounds fixed.
lessons: Score an agent on what the engine actually does with its decision, not on the label it chose.
A check that every policy passes the same way measures the engine, not the policy; keep it out of the policy's score.
False alarms must be counted on every case, or a policy that forbids everything looks good.
Avoid known names in planted traps, or the suite measures name matching.
risks: Scoring the label a policy chose instead of what the engine does with it.
Counting false alarms only on control cases, which rewards a policy that forbids everything.
Planted column names that match known precedents, so the suite measures name matching.
A 'scripted' suite quietly calling a live model through stage notes when a key is present.
Checks every policy passes the same way, inflating a bad policy's score.
